plan.english: Let your blood grow with blood.

cognate_refs.locus: KUB 9.4 i 17–18 (+ KUB 55.20; CTH 760 per West 2007 ch. 8 n. 68, filed under CTH 409 in TLH)

notes: The 'blood to blood' polyptoton with the same heteroclitic noun in both branches: AV ásṛk ... asnā́ (nom. + instr.), Hittite ešḫar=kan ešḫani ḫandan 'blood is fitted to blood' (nom. + dat.-loc.), in the list bone-sinew-blood that Watkins (1995: 529) and West (2007 ch. 8) compare with Merseburg II bluot zi bluoda (OHG bluot is not cognate). Instrumental follows the Vedic. The verb is interpolated: h₁léwdʰeti continues Vedic rohatu (ruh- < *h₁lewdʰ- 'grow'); Hittite has ḫandai- 'fit'. The enclitic 'your' (Ved. te) is interpolated. Locus corrected in round 2 (DCS checked): the polyptoton ásṛk … asnā́ stands in the Paippalāda text (AVP 4.15.3); the Śaunaka AVŚ 4.12.4 has ásṛk te ásthi rohatu 'let your blood, your bone grow' without the instrumental.

plan.english: Set marrow with marrow; let your blood grow with blood.

cognate_refs.locus: KUB 9.4 i 17–18 (+ KUB 55.20; CTH 760 per West 2007 ch. 8 n. 68, filed under CTH 409 in TLH)
Contra vermes (Munich ms., Braune–Helm Ahd. Lesebuch no. 89)

notes: Marrow to marrow, blood to blood. Marrow: AVŚ 4.12.4a majjā́ majjñā́ sáṃ dhīyatām (DCS checked); Watkins's key word of the inherited list of the body's constituents (1995: 523–34). Weak, kept with that warning: the marrow word is root-level only (Ved. n-stem majján- against the thematic *mosgʰó- of Germanic, Avestan and Slavic, the lexeme used), and no second branch has a marrow-to-marrow phrase: the OHG nesso charm (not in local corpora) has only 'out of the marrow', support only. Blood as in healing-charms-001 (AVP 4.15.3 ásṛk te asnā́, DCS checked; Hittite ešḫar=kan ešḫani, TLH checked), the line's one secure element. The active imperative 'set!' of dʰeh₁ follows chinnáṃ sáṃ dhehi 'set together what is severed (o herb)' of AVŚ 4.12.5 (round 1 cited 4.12.7; stanza count from the DCS text), since the engine has no 3sg middle imperative for sáṃ dhīyatām; Vedic only, interpolated; sám 'together' has no usable lexeme and is left out.

Watkins's proto-text of the IE charm (1995: 534): the slaying verb *gʷʰen- linked by contiguity with the list ending in MARROW (*mosgʰo-) in India (AVŚ 12.5.70 majjā́nam asya nír jahi 'strike out his marrow', DCS checked; round 1 cited majjñáḥ), Germanic (nesso charm: worm driven out from the marrow) and Ireland (gono míl 'I slay the beast'). Weak: a reconstruction by contiguity; the OHG and Old Irish refs each contribute one word and are not in local corpora; marrow is root-level (Ved. n-stem). Vedic jahi is the 2sg imperative of the athematic present (gʷʰénti). 'Out' is interpolated with úd (Ved. nír has no usable etymon); 'his' with the demonstrative (Ved. asya).

The worm charm's paean in the 1st singular present: AV vaḥ krimayo hanmi 'I slay you, o worms' and Old Irish gono mil 'I slay the beast' (the only attestation of the 1sg absolute of gonaid), 'two performances of the same text' (Watkins 1995: 520–2; West 2007 ch. 8). Both are the athematic 1sg *gʷʰénmi. The objects are not cognate (kṛ́mi- 'worm' vs mil 'beast' ~ Gk μῆλον), and neither 'worm' nor *meh₁lo- is a usable lexeme, so only the Vedic enclitic 'you (pl.)' is kept, interpolated.

The words that close a successful cure: AVŚ 4.12.6 práti tiṣṭhordhváḥ 'stand firm upright', said to the healed patient (DCS checked; round 1 cited 4.12.7, stanza count from the DCS text), and Pindar's Asclepius who set his patients on their feet, ἔστασεν ὀρθούς (Pyth. 3.53; not in local corpora; West 2007 ch. 8). Weak, kept with that warning: same root *steh₂- in both, but Vedic has the reduplicated present imperative and Greek the transitive s-aorist ('set them upright'), so the verb is root-level; *h₃r̥dʰwó- against ὀρθός (ϝορθ-) is itself debated; common words, a thematic parallel. The root-aorist imperative is the lexicon's form. próti (Ved. práti) is Vedic only, interpolated.

cognate_refs.locus: KUB 9.4 i 16 (+ KUB 55.20; TLH CTH 409, KUB 55.20+ Vs. I 16)

notes: 'Bone to bone' (review P9; West 2007 ch. 8; Watkins 1995: 523–34): the polyptoton of the word for 'bone', nominative with an oblique case of the same noun, in the Paippalāda healing hymn (AVP 4.15.2 asthnā́sthy ápi rohatu 'let bone grow (together) with bone', DCS checked) and in the Hittite ritual (ḫaštai=kan ḫaštai ḫandan 'bone is fitted to bone', KUB 55.20+ Vs. I 16 in TLH, checked; the next lines have 'sinew to sinew' and 'blood to blood', see healing-charms-001). Ved. ásthi- and Hitt. ḫaštai- both continue the PIE word for bone (*h₃ésth₁, Hittite with an -ai- extension, Kloekhorst). Instrumental follows the Vedic (Hittite has the dative-locative). The verb is interpolated: h₁léwdʰeti continues Vedic rohatu (ruh- 'grow', as in healing-charms-001); Hittite has ḫandai- 'fit'. Support only: AVŚ 4.12.3 sám ásthy ápi rohatu (bone without the polyptoton, DCS checked) and Merseburg II ben zi bena (OHG bein is not cognate; not in local corpora). Limit: the lexicon records no Hittite reflex of *h₃ésth₁, so the builder's check can credit the bone word in the Vedic branch only, although the Hittite cognate stands in the passage.

Round 3 draft (docs/audits/tier2-round3-drafts.md), from the formula witness scan (docs/research/formula-witness-scan.md); not yet reviewed. West 2007 ch. 8 (west_ch08_f23): 'stand upright' as the result of healing. Vedic AVŚ 4.12.6 sá út tiṣṭha … práti tiṣṭhordhváḥ 'stand up … stand firm, upright' (the Rohiṇī bone-healing charm; DCS chapter 'AVŚ, 4, 12' has no stanza counters, so the stanza was counted: it is the sixth of seven, Whitney's 4.12.6). Greek Pind. Pyth. 3.53 τοὺς δὲ τομαῖς ἔστασεν ὀρθούς 'others he set upright with surgery' (Asclepius; GLAUx 0033-002). Adjective: ὀρθός = ūrdhvá- (*h₃r̥dʰwós), exact in Greek; the builder gives the Vedic only root level (mapping gap for AV ūrdhva). Verb: root level in both: Vedic tiṣṭha is the reduplicated present imperative (*stísteh₂-, the lexicon's stísteh₂ti is not usable), Greek ἔστασεν the transitive s-aorist 'made stand'. The line uses the intransitive root aorist imperative *sth₂dʰí (Gk στῆθι), which matches the Vedic voice and mood, not its stem; so the Greek causative construction is not reproduced. The Homeric posture collocation ὀρθὸς στῆ (Il. 23.271) ~ RV ūrdhvás tasthau (1.164.10b) is generic and is not used.
